title: Maxwell's Demon and the Physics of Information
question: Could a tiny intelligent being sort molecules and beat the second law of thermodynamics, and what does the answer reveal about information?
summary: Maxwell's demon seemed to break the second law by sorting fast and slow molecules. The resolution, via Landauer's principle, is that erasing information costs energy, showing that information is physical.
content:
A Thought Experiment That Wouldn't Die

In 1867, James Clerk Maxwell imagined a tiny being guarding a trapdoor between two chambers of gas. Whenever a fast molecule approached from the left, the demon opened the door to let it through; whenever a slow one approached from the right, it did the same. Over time the right chamber would grow hot and the left cold, without any work being done. This would violate the second law of thermodynamics, the principle that entropy in an isolated system never decreases. Maxwell's point was that the second law is statistical, not absolute. But his demon raised a sharper question that took more than a century to answer: what, exactly, stops it?

Measurement Is Not Free... Or Is It?

The first serious answer came from Leo Szilard in 1929. He simplified the setup to a single molecule in a box and argued that the demon's act of measuring which side the molecule was on must generate at least kBT ln 2 of entropy, exactly enough to cancel the work it could extract. Later, Léon Brillouin argued that the demon needs light to see molecules, and photons carry entropy. For decades, the consensus was that measurement itself has an unavoidable thermodynamic cost.

That consensus turned out to be wrong. In the 1970s and 80s, Charles Bennett, building on Rolf Landauer's work at IBM, showed that measurement can, in principle, be done reversibly with no entropy cost. The real price lies elsewhere.

Landauer's Principle: Forgetting Costs Energy

Landauer argued in 1961 that erasing information is irreducibly physical: wiping one bit of memory must dissipate at least kBT ln 2 of heat into the environment. Bennett saw that this rescues the second law. The demon must record each molecule's speed to decide whether to open the door. Its memory is finite, so eventually it must erase old records to keep working. That erasure dumps exactly the entropy the demon had removed from the gas. The demon is not defeated by seeing; it is defeated by forgetting.

This resolution has been tested. In 2012, a team led by Antoine Bérut and Eric Lutz trapped a colloidal bead in a double-well laser potential and measured the heat released when erasing one bit, confirming Landauer's bound. Other experiments have built real "information engines" that convert knowledge about a particle's position into work, exactly as Szilard imagined.

Information Is Physical

The deepest lesson of Maxwell's demon is Landauer's slogan: information is physical. Bits are not abstractions floating above matter; they are stored in physical states and governed by thermodynamics. Thermodynamic entropy and Shannon's information entropy are not just mathematically similar, they are two faces of the same quantity. A demon's knowledge is a resource, like fuel, and losing it has a cost.

This insight now shapes modern physics and computing. It sets a fundamental lower limit on the energy cost of irreversible computation, motivates research into reversible and adiabatic computing, informs the thermodynamics of living cells (which act like molecular demons, sorting ions and copying DNA), and even appears in debates about black hole information. A whimsical creature guarding a door ended up revealing that the universe keeps accounts in bits.

perspectives.title: Thermodynamic Perspective
perspectives.description: The second law is statistical. The demon highlights that entropy accounting must include every part of the system, including the demon's own internal state and memory.

perspectives.title: Information Theory Perspective
perspectives.description: Shannon entropy and thermodynamic entropy are linked by Boltzmann's constant. Knowledge about a system is a resource that can be converted into work, and erasing it carries a minimum cost.

perspectives.title: Computer Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Landauer's limit sets a floor on the energy of irreversible logic operations. Reversible computing aims to approach zero dissipation by never discarding information.

perspectives.title: Biological Perspective
perspectives.description: Molecular machines like ion pumps, ribosomes, and DNA polymerases behave like demons, using free energy to sort and copy information. Life may be understood as a thermodynamic information-processing system.

perspectives.title: Philosophical Perspective
perspectives.description: The century-long history of wrong answers shows how subtle the concept of 'information' is, and raises questions about whether physics is ultimately about things or about bits.

connections: The second law of thermodynamics and the arrow of time
openQuestions: How does Landauer's principle generalize to quantum systems, where measurement disturbs what is measured?
Can practical computers ever approach the Landauer limit, and would reversible computing be worth its overhead?
Is information more fundamental than matter and energy, or merely a useful description of physical states?
How close do biological molecular machines come to the thermodynamic limits of information processing?
